item.title: Go Daily Question 20250601
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

var p *int

func foo() (*int, error) {
    var i int = 5
    return &i, nil
}

func bar() {
    //use p
    fmt.Println(*p)
}

func main() {
    p, err := foo()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Println(err)
        return
    }
    bar()
    fmt.Println(*p)
}

A. 5 5 B. runtime error

🔑 Answer Analysis:

B The global *p is nil. In p, err := foo(), p here is a new local variable and is unrelated to the global p.

item.title: Go Daily Question 20250515
item.description:
What code should be filled in at A and B below to ensure the result is printed successfully?

type S struct {
    m string
}

func f() *S {
    return __  //A
}

func main() {
    p := __    //B
    fmt.Println(p.m) //print "foo"
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

A. &S{“foo”} B. *f() or f()

The f() function returns a pointer type, so & can be used to get the pointer to the struct. For B, if *f() is filled in, p is of type S; if f() is filled in, p is of type *S. However, in both cases, p.m can be used to access the struct member.

item.title: Go Daily Question 088
item.description:

  }

}

🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: B

  • The return result can sometimes be a constant;
  • Sometimes function parameters are not evaluated, meaning the return value is determined at compile time;

Here, len(x.s[99]) Since the slice type of s is [][32]byte, len(x.s[99]) = 32.

item.title: Go Daily Question 075
item.description:
What does the following code snippet output?

type Person struct {
    age int
}

func main() {
    person := &Person{28}

    // 1. 
    defer fmt.Println(person.age)

    // 2.
    defer func(p *Person) {
        fmt.Println(p.age)
    }(person)  

    // 3.
    defer func() {
        fmt.Println(person.age)
    }()

    person.age = 29
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

29 29 28 defer is Last-In, First-Out (LIFO). Therefore, // 3 will run first, outputting 29. Then // 2 runs. Here, a pointer type is passed, so the data is also 29. Finally, // 1 runs. Because the value of the parameter is determined when the defer statement is executed, it outputs 28.

item.title: Go Daily Question 058
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

    *p++
    return *p
}

func main() {
    p :=1
    incr(&p)
    fmt.Println(p)
}
  • A. 1
  • B. 2
  • C. 3
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: B.

item.title: Go Daily Question 026
item.description:
Will the following code compile?

package main

import "fmt"

type Student struct {
    Name string
}

var list map[string]Student

func main() {

    list = make(map[string]Student)

    student := Student{"Aceld"}

    list["student"] = student
    list["student"].Name = "LDB"

    fmt.Println(list["student"])
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: Compilation fails. The value of map[string]Student is a Student struct value, so when list["student"] = student, it’s a value copy process. However, list["student"] then becomes a value reference. The characteristic of a value reference is that it is read-only. Therefore, modifying list["student"].Name = "LDB" is not allowed.

item.title: Go Daily Question 007
item.description:
Will the following code compile?

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    m := make(map[string]int)

    fmt.Println(&m["qcrao"])
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: No, it will cause a compilation error.

.\main.go:8:15: invalid operation: cannot take address of m[“qcrao”] (map index expression of type int)

Analysis: This question is equivalent to asking: can you directly take the address of a map’s element?

Key takeaway: You cannot directly take the address of a map's key or value. Even if you obtain the address of a key or value through other “hacky” methods, such as unsafe.Pointer, you cannot hold it long-term because once the map resizes, the positions of keys and values change, and the previously saved addresses become invalid.

item.title: Go Daily Question 012
item.description:
Will the following code compile? If not, what is the reason? If it compiles, what will be the output?

func main() {
    list := new([]int)
    list = append(list, 1)
    fmt.Println(list)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

It will not compile. After new([]int), list is a pointer of type *[]int, and you cannot perform an append operation on a pointer. You can use make() to initialize it first. Similarly, it is recommended to initialize maps and channels using make() or literal syntax, and not new().

item.title: Go Daily Question 019
item.description:
Will the following code compile? If not, what is the reason? If it compiles, what will be the output?

func main() {
    list := new([]int)
    list = append(list, 1)
    fmt.Println(list)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: Cannot compile. The type of list is a pointer of type *[]int. The first parameter of append must be a slice, not the address of a slice.

You can initialize it with make() before use. Similarly, for map and channel, it is recommended to initialize them using make() or literal syntax, and not new().
